source.title: Optimizing loss functions through multi-variate taylor polynomial parameterization

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, though its opening identifies it as under review at ICLR 2021 while the provided venue is GECCO 2020.
record.tranche_reason: Reports that changing the loss function can improve test accuracy and that the gain is especially pronounced on reduced training data, refining how training choices affect generalization. It does not test the claim's random-label memorization premise.
record.gate_note: Tests the effects of evolved loss functions and evaluation length on test accuracy. Rows do not establish whether networks that fit random labels generalize on natural labels; the paper reports no random-label experiment.
record.test_reason: The study compares evolved loss functions with cross-entropy, which tests none of V1–V8. Its two-model accuracy-basin illustration does not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness, training-to-test gaps, or ranking against other generalization measures. General improvements in test accuracy do not establish any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the authors' conclusion: TaylorGLO makes loss-function search more efficient and produces losses that improve test accuracy, data utilization, and model robustness, with particular benefits on reduced datasets. Qualify the empirical summary: two Table 1 comparisons are not significant, and discouraging overfitting is the authors' proposed explanation rather than a directly isolated mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: Optimizes a multivariate Taylor-polynomial loss using CMA-ES and evaluates candidate losses by partial model training; not a test of random-label memorization or the versioned interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Candidate evaluation length changes sample efficiency and the reported test result: 200-step and 20,000-step evaluations were less sample efficient than the main 2,000-step evaluations. Gains vary across model and Cutout settings; the CIFAR-10 Wide ResNet 28-5 comparisons are not statistically significant.

fits_no_version.finding: TaylorGLO improves test accuracy over cross-entropy significantly in 11 of 13 Table 1 settings; neither CIFAR-10 Wide ResNet 28-5 comparison is significant. Reduced-data experiments also favor TaylorGLO.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizing loss functions can improve image-classification test accuracy, including with limited training data.

fits_no_version.finding: Losses evolved with 200-step or 20,000-step candidate evaluations yield slightly lower and more variable final accuracy than the main 2,000-step run; the authors also report worse search efficiency.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Candidate-evaluation length affects loss-function search efficiency and resulting test accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6.2 and Figure 4 describe a flatter, lower accuracy basin for TaylorGLO than cross-entropy in two AllCNN-C models. No magnitude-aware sharpness statistic or training-to-test gap comparison is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Evolved loss functions can improve robustness to weight perturbations in an illustrated two-dimensional slice.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Conference on Genetic and Evolutionary Computation (provided venue); supplied text also says 'Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2021'.
record.problems: The claim's key random-label and capacity relationship is not tested. The reduced-data comparison reports only four successful cross-entropy runs and gives no standard deviation for their accuracy. Several TaylorGLO versus cross-entropy differences on CIFAR-10 are not statistically significant. The loss-function evolution evaluates candidates on validation data and selects the highest validation score.
record.rows_left_out: None of the reported outcome results relevant to this paper's loss-function intervention were left out; the paper does not report additional measured outcomes that test versions V1–V8.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization; random-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Dropout interventions, dropout strength, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus training-to-test gaps among similarly fitted models, and comparison with norm- and margin-based rankings.
Retraining after removing highly memorized versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Replace the record's tests/T5 classification: loss-function improvements do not revise any listed version. The basin illustration is related to V7 but does not test its specified relationship. Dropout benefits mentioned in the discussion are attributed to prior work. The supplied text identifies arXiv:2002.00059v4 under ICLR 2021 review; its correspondence to the supplied DOI is not established here.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or natural-label generalization comparison.
No width sweep across the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer comparison.
No dropout ablation; the paper notes that the MNIST basic CNN includes dropout but does not compare dropout settings.
No magnitude-aware sharpness comparison or ranking of generalization measures.
